title: Backpressure simulated replay harness
content:
Purpose and scope:
This note describes a throughput benchmarking harness that replays captured client traces while intentionally simulating server-side backpressure. The goal is to exercise the serving runtime under realistic arrival patterns and to validate graceful degradation, prioritization, and queueing behavior without needing production traffic. Unlike earlier warmup/playbooks, this doc focuses on:
- faithful time-replay of client pacing (inter-arrival and token pacing)
- injecting controlled backpressure (CPU/GPU throttles, artificial Q-depth limits)
- measuring repeatability with deterministic seeds and traffic-conditioning primitives

Why backpressure-focused replay?
Common throughput regressions only manifest when request concurrency and queueing interact with kernel stalls, memory thrash, or scheduling. Pure synthetic Poisson or steady-state generators miss these queuing dynamics. Replaying real traces while imposing configurable throttles reveals tail amplification and cascading latency spikes.

High-level design
- Capture: collect lightweight client-side traces (arrival timestamp, prompt size/tokens, route/model id, client-id, idempotency key, optional prompt-hash). Add server-side telemetry correlation id when available.
- Normalize: convert timestamps to relative deltas and collapse inactive periods (user-think) into configurable multipliers.
- Replay engine: read normalized trace and emit requests with original inter-arrival timings. Optionally apply token-level pacing to emulate streaming clients (per-token inter-packet spacing).
- Backpressure injector: an adapter layer that can simulate three modes: 1) per-model concurrency cap (max inflight), 2) artificial service-time multiplier (sleep on server stub), 3) GPU bandwidth limiter (throttle outgoing tokens). The injector sits between loadgen and real serving endpoints or a local stub.
- Metrics collector: client latencies (p50/p90/p99), server queue depth over time, GPU util, memory high-water, kernel time breakdown, and error counts (429, 503, timeouts). Correlate by request id.

Trace capture recommendations
- Minimal fields: unix-ts-ms, route, prompt-token-count, response-token-expected, client-id (or traffic segment), request-id, seed (if present).
- Capture at sampling rate 1:100 for production traces to reduce PII surface; for targeted experiments capture full traces in staging.
- Redact PII before exporting. Store prompt-hash for content-length fidelity.
- Save both wall clock and monotonic deltas to support both time-replay and scale-agnostic replay.

Normalization rules (repeatability hygiene)
- Convert absolute timestamps to relative deltas from trace start.
- Replace client-id with segment labels (e.g., web, mobile, api-batch) to avoid sensitive identifiers.
- Collapse idle gaps > T_idle_cutoff into a single gap marker with a multiplier (configurable) so experiments can simulate longer runs without huge idle spans.
- Deterministic seed: each replay must set RNG seed for sampling decisions (trace sub-sampling, jitter, synthetic prompt mutation). Seed value must be stored in the experiment manifest.

Backpressure injection modes and controls
1) concurrency-cap: enforce server-side inflight limit N. When N is reached, loadgen receives 429/queue-backoff errors or stalls according to configured policy (drop vs retry vs enqueue at client). Use this to evaluate client backoff logic and server prioritization.
Parameters: max_inflight (int), backoff_policy (none|linear|exponential), client-retry-limit (int).
2) service-time-multiplier: multiply nominal server processing time by factor f to emulate slow downstreams. Implemented as an interceptor that sleeps or fields longer kernel waits. Useful for kernel-level contention tests.
Parameters: multiplier (float), latency-jitter-ms (int).
3) resource-throttle: simulate slower GPU memory bandwidth or reduced batch throughput by limiting tokens-per-second emitted by the server stub.
Parameters: tps_limit, max_batch_size, enforced_queue_delay_ms.

Load generator config knobs
- arrival-mode: real-time | speedup (x times faster than real) | occupancy-driven (target average queue depth)
- token-pacing: none | per-request (burst) | streaming (per-token inter-packet ms)
- seed: integer (required)
- target-duration: seconds
- warmup-window: seconds (see warmup section)
- error-handling: fail-fast | record-and-continue | adaptive-backoff
- histogram-window: seconds for rolling latency histogram aggregation

Warmup strategy (conditional)
Rationale: warmup isn't just about model priming — we want the runtime's memory and kernel paths warmed to avoid first-request spikes but not overprime caches that hide real-world cold behavior.
Recommended multi-stage warmup:
1) micro-prime (30–60s): tiny requests (short prompts) at low concurrency to initialize kernels and memory pools.
2) occupancy ramp (2–5min): slowly increase arrival rate to target concurrency while keeping token sizes representative. Watch for memory allocations and CUDA driver bumps.
3) stress-pulse (60–120s): short burst exceeding target concurrency by 1.5–2x to surface scheduling behaviors and queue saturation.
4) stabilization (2–10min): let the system run at target throughput and check that P50 stabilizes within expected band and no recurrent OOMs or eviction patterns occur.
Log warmup seeds and snapshot server telemetry at each boundary.

Repeatability and experiment manifest
Every run must produce a JSON manifest (store alongside trace) containing: trace-id, seed, arrival-mode, backpressure-mode (if any), max_inflight, multiplier, tps_limit, warmup-seconds, created_by, git-commit (loadgen), server-image, experiment-tags. This manifest is critical for re-running and auditing.
Deterministic artifacts:
- random seeds
- software version hashes
- trace normalization parameters

Measurement windows and metrics definitions
- warmup_window: exclude from final metrics. Record metrics during warmup too for diagnostics but only report steady-state values post-warmup-window.
- steady_state_window: recommended 5–15 minutes depending on cadence.
- throughput (tokens/s): server-side counted emitted tokens / steady_state_window.
- goodput (completed requests/s): requests that finished without 5xx/timeout.
- latency metrics: client-observed request latency p50/p90/p95/p99 and server-queue-wait p50/p90/p99. Capture per-token latencies for streaming tests.
- queue depth: instantaneous inflight request count sampled at 1s. Report mean and tail.
- error rate: percent requests resulting in 4xx/5xx/timeouts.

Analysis and repeatability checks
- seed drift: re-run identical manifest 3 times. Acceptable variance: p50 < 5% CV, p90 < 10% CV; if outside, investigate nondeterministic components (autoscaling, background jobs, noisy neighbors).
- KS test for latency distributions: compare baseline run distribution to candidate run; flag if p < 0.01.
- regression windows: compute moving-window percent change across time to detect drift during long runs (e.g., >10% throughput drop sustained for 3 windows).

Common failure modes and mitigations
- drift due to cloud autoscaler kicks: pin node pools for critical runs or run on dedicated capacity.
- warmup over-priming hides cold-path regressions: keep an experiment variant with minimal warmup to track first-request regressions.
- trace sampling bias: ensure segments (web/mobile/api) are proportionally represented. Validate with simple chi-squared on client-id segments.
- measurement clock skew: always use monotonic deltas for inter-arrival and server-side monotonic timestamps for queueing metrics.

Practical tips and scripts
- store manifests in GCS path: gs://redwood-loadtests/<date>/<trace-id>/<manifest>.json
- standard seed selection: hash(trace-id)+YYYYMMDD -> seed integer. This ties seed to trace but still allows day-based reproducibility.
- use low-overhead exporters: compress telemetry windows (1s) and only expand during failure analysis.
- when injecting concurrency-cap, log exact enqueue/reject events to a separate file for postmortem queue-occupancy reconstruction.

Experiment template (copy/remove fields when running)
- experiment-name: string
- trace-id: string
- seed: integer
- arrival-mode: real-time|speedup=10|occupancy-driven
- backpressure-mode: none|concurrency-cap|max_inflight=24|service-time-multiplier=1.8|resource-throttle=tps=12000
- warmup-seconds: int
- steady-state-seconds: int
- run-notes: string (what we changed vs baseline)
- expected-sla: p99 < X ms, goodput > Y req/s

Example quickstart command (pseudo):
./loadgen replay --trace ./traces/ui-shopping-20251115.json --seed 12345 --arrival-mode speedup=5 --token-pacing streaming:20ms --backpressure concurrency-cap:24 --warmup 300 --steady 900 --manifest ./out/exp-xxx-manifest.json

Post-run checklist
- upload manifest and raw telemetry to GCS
- generate latency/queue depth plots (include warmup markers)
- run repeatability script (rerun x3) if regression suspected
- create issue with links to manifest, plots, and run artifacts if regression confirmed

Open questions and next steps
- integrate trace anonymization into telemetry pipeline to allow safe higher-fidelity captures.
- add an occupancy-driven controller that adjusts injected throttle to maintain a target queue depth as a stress mode.
- standardize KS/AD statistical thresholds in shared metrics lib for automated alerts.

Appendix: quick diagnostics to run when p90 jumps
1) check GPU util and memory HWM around jump timestamp
2) inspect queue-enqueue/reject logs for sudden spikes in 429/503
3) cross-check with infra events (node reboots, autoscaler actions)
4) re-run a short isolated trace (isolated model, small token sizes) to see if regression is model-specific

Notes to self / TODOs:
- wire up automatic manifest generation in CI loadgen runner
- add a canned dashboard for backpressure experiments with warmup/steady-state overlays

End of doc.
